01
How the efficiency works
We make the parts once, then assemble them into everything.
Traditional production builds each asset from scratch. Modular production builds the components once, then recombines them into every format, channel and market that needs them. The saving compounds every time something new is asked for.

Every piece of work takes one of three routes.
You always know which one.
At briefing we choose a route for each deliverable. The route decides how much of the production sequence our people run and how much the system runs. It never changes who approves the work.

04
Modularity
A brief only uses the parts of the system it needs.
MAKE is a set of modules, not one product you switch on whole. A single social cut-down touches two of them. A nine-market campaign touches all of them. There is nothing to implement twice, and nothing for your team to learn about the parts a brief never uses.
The module set
One connected space
AI tasks
Open integrations
Global e‑commerce

Each module handles a different part of production. A module is switched on for a brief or it is not. There is no partial state and no second implementation underneath.

06
Why the integration matters
Integrating your DAM is what stops the same
asset being made twice.
Your library already holds a great deal of what the next brief needs, but today nothing asks it before production starts. Integrating it turns your DAM from a store of finished files into your brand’s intelligence layer: a live record of what exists, what each asset is made of and where it has been used.

08
What it means in practice
Your second market orders what already exists.
It does not brief again.
Because every brief leaves its components and a record behind, the next market can search, find and order. Language, format and local claims become choices on a form rather than a new brief, a new schedule and a new cost.
Instead of this
A second brief, a second concept, a second shoot, a second review.
The whole chain on page 07 run again, at close to full cost and full timeline, to produce something that is a near neighbour of an asset already sitting in your DAM.
This happens instead
Step 1
Search your DAM
Your second market looks in the system they already use, for work that already exists.
Step 2
See what carries over
Six of the nine components from the first market carry straight across. Three are market-specific and get replaced.
Step 3
Place an order
Language   local
Formats   9:16, banner
Local claims   applied
A form, not a brief.
Step 4
Approved and delivered
Same approval gate as any other route, then delivered and registered back, so the third market starts from a larger set again.
Nobody writes a creative brief. Nobody schedules a shoot.   And nobody in the second market needs to know the first market’s production history to place the order. What can be ordered is exactly what the record says already exists.
09
Your existing library
Getting started does not depend on tidying your archive first.
Everything produced from day one is fully described and ready to reorder immediately. For material already in your DAM, we describe it at the point it is first reused, so there is no cataloguing project to finish before the benefit starts.
Everything in your DAM
Already there, described inconsistently
usable, but not yet orderable as components
Produced from day one
complete record,
orderable immediately
this boundary moves every time something is reused
Nothing to do before we start
Your first briefs run from day one. They do not wait on the state of the archive, and they do not depend on it.
Described when it is used
The first time a piece of existing material is reused, we describe it properly, once. From that point it behaves like anything else in the system.
Prioritised only where it pays
If part of your library has obvious demand, we can prepare it ahead of time. We will agree that with you in discovery rather than assume it.
You raised this in the last round, and it is a fair challenge.   The answer is that the value does not sit behind a back-catalogue project. It starts with your first brief and the archive catches up behind it.
